SK5007 A certificate callback that accepts everything

A TLS validation callback that returns true without looking makes the connection encrypted but unauthenticated.

CategorySecurity
Default severityerror
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.1

Why

TLS gives you two things and they are separable: the traffic is encrypted, and the party at the other end is who the certificate says. A callback that returns true for every input keeps the first and throws away the second — so the connection is perfectly encrypted, to whoever answered. That is the whole content of a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker on the path presents any certificate at all, this code accepts it, and reads and rewrites everything in both directions while both ends see a padlock. Deleting the callback restores the platform's validation, which is chain building, revocation, hostname matching and the trust store, and is years of work nobody should reimplement. If one specific self-signed certificate genuinely has to be trusted — a device on a factory network, a local development server — then pin it: compare certificate.GetCertHashString() against the one thumbprint you mean and return false for every other input. That is four lines, it is auditable, and it fails closed when the wrong certificate shows up.

Example

Instead of:

handler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (_, _, _, _) => true;

Write:

handler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = (_, certificate, _, errors) =>
    errors == SslPolicyErrors.None
    || certificate?.GetCertHashString(HashAlgorithmName.SHA256) == PinnedThumbprint;

When it does not fire

Two conditions must both hold, and both are decided without following anything. The target has to be a delegate that returns bool and takes a System.Net.Security.SslPolicyErrors — which is how the rule covers ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback, HttpClientHandler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback, SslClientAuthenticationOptions.RemoteCertificateValidationCallback and the SslStream constructor argument without naming any of them, and how a fifth spelling arrives covered. And the value has to be provably constant-true: an expression body that is the literal true, a block whose one statement is return true;, or HttpClientHandler.DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator. ⚠ A callback with any condition in it is silence — a thumbprint comparison, an errors == SslPolicyErrors.None test, a method group, a field holding a delegate. Following those is the inter-procedural analysis docs/plan/08 puts out of scope, and a wrong error here would fail a build over a pinning implementation. ⚠ The most common true finding is a test or a local development environment talking to a self-signed certificate, and the rule ships at error anyway. That is not the same situation as SK8005's polling Thread.Sleep, which is correct code the rule cannot recognise; this is never correct code, it is an accepted risk — and an accepted risk has a way of reaching production inside a #if that stopped being conditional. Accept it deliberately and visibly: a baseline entry, or a #pragma with a justification comment. ⚠ Nothing enforces that comment today — SK7050 is allocated in docs/plan/08 and unbuilt — so the baseline, whose diff somebody reads, is the disposal with a mechanism behind it. Not a lower severity.
